Inscribed Square 2

GeometryTrianglesConstructions
Game: A square is hiding inside every triangle; this is a picture to explore, with nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Drag the three corner dots, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes for names and helper lines, and press Reset to start again.

Keyboard: Tab to a dot, then use the arrow keys (Shift makes a bigger step).

Look for the math

Move the triangle and the red square follows. The trick is to build a square outside the triangle first; two lines through the third corner then cut out the one inside.

The construction

Put a square CA-ABCb on the side AB, on the side away from C. Join C to the two far corners Ca and Cb. Those lines cross AB at P and Q. Raise perpendiculars at P and Q; they meet AC and BC at P' and Q'. The page claims PQ is the base of the wanted square. The logic test checked that claim on an exact triangle, a 972-position grid (735 usable positions; the applet's own parallel test rejects the rest) and 4,000 rotated random triangles: all four sides match whenever the lines meet.

Why the sides come out equal

Let L be the length of AB and h the altitude from C. Three pairs of similar triangles share the segments CP, CCa, CQ and CCb, so their side ratios are all the same. The result is a square of side s = L·h / (L + h), whatever the shape of the triangle. When the foot of the altitude falls between A and B, all four vertices lie on the three sides, not just on the lines through them.

One scale, two centres

The small square is a homothety of the Vecten square with centre C and scale h / (L + h) = s / L. So the two square centres c1, c2 and C lie on one line; the test measured the missing area of that line on every case and found errors below 1e-8. Tick "Extra info" to see those centres, the two diagonals of each square and the line joining them. The same line passes through a Vecten point of the triangle, which the test also checked on the grid triangles.

The second solution

The page says there are in general two solutions, from an outward and an inward Vecten square. The applet only shows the outward one. If the square is built on the same side of AB as C, the same construction gives another square of side L·h / |L − h|; the test verified it on the inward grid. For h < L its top lies past C, so it is a square on the sidelines, outside the triangle. When h = L two lines are parallel and the construction breaks down. The live cut-the-knot page now shows a still image instead of the Java applet; an archived 2012 copy embedded InscribedSquare2 with the explanation's ShowNames=1, which is why the names start on here.

Try dragging C until its altitude is close to the length of AB, then tick "Extra info" and watch the two centres shoot apart.
